title.en: The invisible living world: microscopes and cells

text.en: A water-filled flask makes letters on a page look bigger, just like a magnifying glass. Can lenses show us a hidden living world?

The human eye cannot see very small things, but lenses, shaped like a lentil seed, thick in the middle and thin at the edge, can magnify them.
Robert Hooke looked at thin cork under a microscope in the 1660s and saw many small empty boxes, which he called cells.
Antonie van Leeuwenhoek made better lenses and was the first to describe bacteria and blood cells.
All living beings are made of cells, which are the basic units of life.
To see an onion peel cell, we stain a thin peel with safranin, place it on a slide with glycerin and a cover slip, and view it under a microscope.
A plant cell has a cell wall outside, then a cell membrane, cytoplasm and a nucleus.
The nucleus regulates activities and growth of the cell, and the cell wall gives plants rigidity and strength.
Plant cells also have plastids such as chloroplasts, which contain chlorophyll for photosynthesis, and a large vacuole for storage.
Animal cells have no cell wall, and have small or no vacuoles.
Some organisms are just one cell, such as amoeba or bacteria, while others, like us, are made of many cells.

problem.en: Name three parts found in both plant and animal cells and one found only in plants.

text.en: Both have a cell membrane, cytoplasm and a nucleus.
Plant cells also have a cell wall.
They also have chloroplasts in green parts.

prompt.en: How do plant and animal cells differ?

requiredIdeas.en: Plant cells have a cell wall and chloroplasts.

commonMisconceptions.en: Animal cells have a cell wall.

points.en: Hooke named cells and Leeuwenhoek saw microbes.
Cells have a membrane, cytoplasm and nucleus; plants add a wall and chloroplasts.
Living things may be single-celled or many-celled.
